title: Chapter 34 — The Cabin-Table
paragraphs: It is noon, and Dough-Boy, the steward, thrusts his pale bread-dough face from the cabin hatch to announce dinner to his lord and master. Ahab, sitting in the lee quarter-boat, has just been taking a reading of the sun and is now silently calculating the latitude on the smooth, medallion-shaped tablet reserved for this daily purpose on the upper part of his ivory leg. From his complete inattention to the news, you'd think moody Ahab hadn't heard his servant. But presently, catching hold of the mizzen shrouds, he swings himself to the deck and, in an even, unenthusiastic voice, says, "Dinner, Mr. Starbuck," and disappears into the cabin.

When the last echo of his sultan's step has faded and Starbuck, the first Emir, has every reason to believe he is seated, then Starbuck rouses from his stillness, takes a few turns along the deck, and after a grave peep into the binnacle (the compass housing), says with some touch of pleasantness, "Dinner, Mr. Stubb," and goes below. The second Emir lounges about the rigging a while, then slightly shakes the main brace, to see whether all is well with that important rope. He likewise takes up the old refrain and, with a quick "Dinner, Mr. Flask," follows his predecessors.

But the third Emir, now finding himself all alone on the quarter-deck, seems to feel freed from some odd restraint; for, tossing off all kinds of knowing winks in every direction and kicking off his shoes, he breaks into a quick but silent squall of a hornpipe right over the Grand Turk's head; and then, with a deft trick, tossing his cap up into the mizzentop to use as a shelf, he goes below, rollicking — at least as long as he stays visible from the deck — reversing all other processions by bringing up the rear with the music. But before stepping through the cabin doorway below, he stops, puts on a completely new face, and then independent, hilarious little Flask enters King Ahab's presence in the role of Abjectus, or the Slave.

It is not the least among the strange things bred by the intense artificiality of sea customs that, while on the open deck some officers will, when provoked, carry themselves boldly and defiantly enough toward their commander, yet, ten to one, let those very officers go down the next moment to their customary dinner in that same commander's cabin, and at once their inoffensive, not to say apologetic and humble, air toward him as he sits at the head of the table is marvelous, and sometimes most comical. Why this difference? A problem? Perhaps not. To have been Belshazzar, King of Babylon, and to have been Belshazzar not haughtily but courteously — in that there certainly must have been some touch of worldly grandeur. But the man who presides in a rightly regal and intelligent spirit over his own private dinner table of invited guests — that man's unchallenged power and dominion of personal influence for the time being, that man's royalty of state, surpasses Belshazzar's, for Belshazzar was not the greatest. Whoever has once had his friends to dinner has tasted what it is to be Caesar. It is a witchery of social czarship that there is no withstanding. Now, if on top of this you add the official supremacy of a ship's captain, then by inference you will arrive at the cause of that peculiarity of sea life just mentioned.

Over his ivory-inlaid table, Ahab presided like a mute, maned sea-lion on the white coral beach, surrounded by his warlike but still deferential cubs. Each officer waited to be served in his own proper turn. They were like little children before Ahab; and yet in Ahab there seemed not to lurk the smallest social arrogance. With one mind, their intent eyes all fastened on the old man's knife as he carved the chief dish before him. I do not suppose that for the world they would have profaned that moment with the slightest remark, even on so neutral a topic as the weather. No! And when, reaching out his knife and fork with the slice of beef locked between them, Ahab thereby motioned Starbuck's plate toward him, the mate received his meat as though receiving alms, and cut it tenderly, and started a little if the knife happened to graze the plate, and chewed it noiselessly, and swallowed it, not without caution. For, like the Coronation banquet at Frankfurt, where the German Emperor dines in profound state with the seven Imperial Electors, these cabin meals were somehow solemn meals, eaten in awful silence; and yet at table old Ahab did not forbid conversation; only he himself was silent. What a relief it was to choking Stubb when a rat made a sudden racket in the hold below. And poor little Flask — he was the youngest son and little boy of this weary family party. His were the shinbones of the salt beef; his would have been the drumsticks. For Flask to have presumed to help himself must have seemed to him the equivalent of larceny in the first degree. Had he helped himself at that table, doubtless he would never again have been able to hold his head up in this honest world; nevertheless, strange to say, Ahab never forbade him. And had Flask helped himself, the chances were that Ahab would never so much as have noticed it. Least of all did Flask presume to help himself to butter. Whether he thought the owners of the ship denied it to him on account of its clotting his clear, sunny complexion, or whether he reckoned that on so long a voyage in such marketless waters butter was at a premium, and therefore not for him, a subordinate — however it was, Flask, alas, was a butterless man!

Another thing: Flask was the last person down to dinner and the first one back up. Consider! This meant Flask's dinner was badly squeezed for time. Starbuck and Stubb both got a head start on him, yet they also had the privilege of lingering. If even Stubb, who ranks only one peg above Flask, happened to have a small appetite and showed signs of finishing his meal, then Flask had to hurry — he wouldn't get more than three mouthfuls that day, for it was against sacred custom for Stubb to leave the table before Flask. Therefore Flask once confided in private that ever since he had risen to the dignity of an officer, he had never known what it was to be anything other than hungry, more or less. What he ate didn't so much relieve his hunger as keep it alive forever. Peace and satisfaction, Flask thought, have departed from my stomach for good. I am an officer — but how I wish I could grab a bit of good old-fashioned beef in the forecastle, the way I used to as a common sailor. There's the fruit of promotion. There's the vanity of glory. There's the insanity of life! Besides, if any ordinary sailor on the Pequod had a grudge against Flask in his official capacity, all that sailor had to do for ample revenge was go aft at dinnertime and peek at Flask through the cabin skylight, sitting there silly and dumbfounded before awful Ahab.

Now, Ahab and his three mates formed what might be called the first table in the Pequod's cabin. After their departure, in reverse order of their arrival, the canvas tablecloth was cleared — or rather restored to some hasty order by the pale steward. Then the three harpooners were invited to the feast, being its residuary legatees — the heirs to whatever was left. They made a sort of temporary servants' hall of the high and mighty cabin.

In strange contrast to the hardly tolerable constraint and nameless invisible domineering of the captain's table was the entire carefree license and ease, the almost frantic democracy, of those inferior fellows the harpooners. While their masters, the mates, seemed afraid of the sound of the hinges of their own jaws, the harpooners chewed their food with such relish that there was a report to it. They dined like lords; they filled their bellies like Indian ships loading with spices all day. Such portentous appetites had Queequeg and Tashtego that, to fill the gaps left by the previous meal, the pale Dough-Boy often had to bring on a great baron of salt-junk (salt beef), seemingly quarried out of the solid ox. And if he was not lively about it, if he did not go with a nimble hop-skip-and-jump, then Tashtego had an ungentlemanly way of speeding him up by darting a fork at his back, harpoon-fashion. And once Daggoo, seized with a sudden humor, assisted Dough-Boy's memory by snatching him up bodily and thrusting his head into a great empty wooden trencher, while Tashtego, knife in hand, began laying out the circle preliminary to scalping him. He was naturally a very nervous, shuddering sort of little fellow, this bread-faced steward, the offspring of a bankrupt baker and a hospital nurse. And what with the standing spectacle of the black, terrifying Ahab and the periodic tumultuous visitations of these three savages, Dough-Boy's whole life was one continual lip-quiver. Usually, after seeing the harpooners furnished with everything they demanded, he would escape from their clutches into his little pantry next door, and fearfully peep out at them through the blinds of its door until it was all over.

It was a sight to see Queequeg seated opposite Tashtego, pitting his filed teeth against the Indian's; crosswise to them, Daggoo sat on the floor, for a bench would have brought his hearse-plumed head up against the low carlines (the beams under the deck overhead); at every motion of his colossal limbs he made the low cabin framework shake, as when an African elephant travels as a passenger in a ship. But for all this, the great negro was wonderfully abstemious, not to say dainty. It seemed hardly possible that by such comparatively small mouthfuls he could keep up the vitality spread through so broad, baronial, and superb a person. But doubtless this noble savage fed strong and drank deep of the abounding element of air, and through his dilated nostrils snuffed in the sublime life of the worlds. Not by beef or by bread are giants made or nourished. But Queequeg — he had a mortal, barbaric smack of the lip in eating, an ugly enough sound, so much so that the trembling Dough-Boy almost looked to see whether any teeth marks lurked in his own lean arms. And when he heard Tashtego singing out for him to show himself, so that his bones might be picked, the simple-witted steward all but shattered the crockery hanging around him in the pantry with his sudden fits of the palsy. Nor did the whetstones the harpooners carried in their pockets for their lances and other weapons — whetstones on which, at dinner, they would ostentatiously sharpen their knives — nor did that grating sound at all tend to calm poor Dough-Boy. How could he forget that in his Island days, Queequeg, for one, must certainly have been guilty of some murderous, convivial indiscretions? Alas, Dough-Boy! Hard fares the white waiter who waits on cannibals. Not a napkin should he carry on his arm, but a buckler. In good time, though, to his great delight, the three salt-sea warriors would rise and depart — to his credulous, fable-mongering ears, all their martial bones jingling in them at every step, like Moorish scimitars in scabbards.

But although these barbarians ate in the cabin and in name lived there, their habits were anything but sedentary, and so they were almost never in it except at mealtimes and just before bed, when they passed through on their way to their own particular quarters.

On this one point Ahab seemed no different from most American whaling captains, who, as a class, tend to think the ship's cabin belongs to them by right, and that anyone else is allowed in it only as a courtesy. So, in plain truth, the mates and harpooners of the Pequod could more accurately be said to have lived outside the cabin than in it. For when they did go in, it was rather the way a street door goes into a house: it swings inward for a moment, only to be swung back out the next, and it lives, permanently, in the open air. Not that they lost much by this; there was no companionship in the cabin; socially, Ahab was unapproachable. Though he was nominally counted in the census of Christendom, he was still a stranger to it. He lived in the world the way the last of the grizzly bears lived in settled Missouri. And just as, when spring and summer had gone, that wild Logan of the woods would bury himself in a hollow tree and live out the winter there, sucking his own paws, so in his harsh, howling old age Ahab's soul, shut up in the hollowed trunk of his body, fed there on the sullen paws of its gloom!
